title: Management of Oromandibular Dystonia: A Case Report and Literature Update
case_prompt:
A 26-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of spontaneous, intermittent, unilateral, paroxysmal, painful involuntary contractions affecting the right half of her face and extending into the right side of her neck. Each episode lasted 3–5 minutes, occurred repetitively throughout the day, and resolved transiently when she consciously opened her mouth. The spasms involved the right forehead, masseter, temporalis, jaw, and neck muscles, were associated with tongue deviation to the left, slurred speech, accidental tongue biting, grimacing, facial flushing, and episodes of breathlessness. Triggers included brushing, eating, touching the right side of her face, talking, and breathing. She reported no relevant medical or neurologic history, but had a past assault to the right side of her face and an uneventful dental extraction six months prior. Previous trials of tricyclic antidepressants and gabapentin provided no relief.

On extraoral examination, fine fasciculations were visible over the right facial region, with a palpable bulge, diffuse swelling, and redness. Intraorally, spasms began as fasciculations in the right masseter and temporalis and progressed within seconds to forceful jaw closure and neck constriction, eliciting a gasping posture; the spasms subsided within 2–3 seconds when the patient forcibly opened her mouth. Temporomandibular joint evaluation showed anterior disc displacement without reduction and excessive anterior movement of the condyle on mouth opening. Neurologic and cranial nerve examinations were otherwise normal.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed no focal lesions. Serum calcium levels were within normal limits. Electromyography of the right masseter and temporalis muscles demonstrated high-frequency, high-voltage motor-unit potentials with sustained or short-duration bursts at rest, whereas the contralateral muscles were electrically silent.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Psychogenic facial spasm was considered because of her psychiatric referrals but was deemed unlikely given that “Patient reports multiple attempts … with no cure; on the contrary she was branded as a psychiatric patient.”  
2. Myokymia was excluded because “Myokymia … is insufficient to move a joint … complete and visible movement of the jaws was taking place in the presenting case.”  
3. Facial myokymia was excluded by imaging: “No focal pathology was detected in MRI of brain.”  
4. Tourette syndrome was unlikely since “Extreme Tourette in adulthood is a rarity.”  
5. Tardive dyskinesias were excluded because the patient had “no previous drug history.”  
6. Hypocalcemic tetany was ruled out as “serum calcium levels were in normal range.”  
7. Facial motor seizures were considered but excluded because “consultation with the neurologic department ruled out other neurologic disorders and this was confirmed by the absence of any other accompanying neurologic deficits.”
